sequences.title: Building the risk-based audit plan

steps.label: List the audit universe
steps.note: Every auditable process, system, site, vendor and legal obligation, at a useful level of detail.

steps.label: Map each entity to risks
steps.note: Link entities to risks and business objectives; management's risk register is one input, not the only one.

steps.label: Rank by current risk
steps.note: Likelihood and impact together, refreshed each cycle, decide what is audited and how often.

steps.label: Audit committee approves the plan
steps.note: Approval covers the plan and the resources needed to deliver it.

steps.label: Adjust for emerging risks
steps.note: An acquisition, new law or major incident triggers a documented update, reported to the audit committee.

sequences.caption: Completeness comes before ranking. Rotation or last year's findings never set the plan on their own; current risk does.

sequences.title: Drawing a statistical sample

steps.label: Set the test objective
steps.note: Decide what the test must show: a deviation rate, a dollar amount, or even one case.

steps.label: Define the population
steps.note: Describe exactly which items the conclusion will cover, matched to the objective.

steps.label: Prove the population is complete
steps.note: Reconcile the extract to the source system, for example by record counts, before sizing anything.

steps.label: Size the sample
steps.note: Confidence, expected errors and the tolerable rate set the size; population size barely matters.

steps.label: Select items at random
steps.note: Every item has an equal chance, so the result can be projected to the population.

steps.label: Evaluate against tolerable rate
steps.note: A clear breach ends reliance on the control; a borderline result calls for a larger sample.

sequences.caption: A sample speaks only for the population it came from. Prove that population is complete before you size or select anything.

sequences.title: Handling suspected fraud during an audit

steps.label: Notice the red flags
steps.note: Stay skeptical: an opportunity, such as sole control of vendor setup, is the visible warning sign.

steps.label: Record the facts
steps.note: Write down objectively what you saw; leave the originals untouched.

steps.label: Escalate to the chief audit executive
steps.note: Follow the fraud-response procedure; go above management to the audit committee if management may be involved.

steps.label: Support the investigators
steps.note: Keep originals under chain of custody for the authorized investigators; run no parallel analysis.

sequences.caption: Document, escalate, then support; preserve originals throughout. Never confront the suspect or widen testing on your own.

sequences.title: Relying on an outside expert's work

steps.label: Confirm a skills gap
steps.note: The subject needs skills the audit team lacks, such as cryptography or actuarial work.

steps.label: Check competence and objectivity
steps.note: Qualifications, experience and any ties to the auditee are assessed before any reliance.

steps.label: Agree the scope in writing
steps.note: Objectives, scope and access are set so the work answers the audit's question.

steps.label: Evaluate the delivered work
steps.note: Check methods, evidence and whether conclusions follow; require fixes or added work if gaps appear.

steps.label: Document how it was used
steps.note: Record what the auditor relied on and why it was judged reliable.

sequences.caption: You can delegate the work, never the responsibility. Credentials earn the expert a hearing; only the evaluated work earns reliance.

sequences.title: Running a control self-assessment

steps.label: Management sponsors the program
steps.note: Management owns control self-assessment (CSA); internal audit may design it, train staff and facilitate.

steps.label: Facilitate owner workshops
steps.note: Open questions draw out the owners' own view of their controls, and dissent is recorded.

steps.label: Rank areas using the results
steps.note: Self-ratings help the auditor see where risk looks highest and where to look first.

steps.label: Test high-risk controls independently
steps.note: The auditor's own testing, not the self-ratings, supports the audit conclusion.

steps.label: Report ratings that tests contradict
steps.note: When self-ratings and test results disagree, the report shows both.

sequences.caption: CSA widens coverage and builds ownership. It guides audit scope, but it never replaces independent testing.

sequences.title: From business strategy to this year's IT plan

steps.label: Start from business strategy
steps.note: IT direction is derived from what the business is trying to achieve, never the reverse.

steps.label: Define the IT target state
steps.note: Describe the capabilities IT must have to support those business goals.

steps.label: Analyze the gaps
steps.note: Compare today's capabilities with the target to see what must be added, changed or retired.

steps.label: Build a prioritized roadmap
steps.note: Order the work over several years; each major investment traces to a measurable business objective.

steps.label: Set the annual tactical plan
steps.note: Turn the roadmap into this year's projects, budgets and milestones.

sequences.caption: Alignment flows down from the business. A material change, such as a merger, triggers a focused, board-endorsed update, not a fresh start.

sequences.title: Creating an IT policy

steps.label: Draft from business objectives
steps.note: A top-down draft keeps the policy aligned with what the enterprise needs.

steps.label: Consult those who must apply it
steps.note: Human resources, legal and business units review the draft, so the rules are workable.

steps.label: Board or top management approves
steps.note: Their approval gives enterprise-wide authority; a functional head's signature cannot.

steps.label: Publish one controlled version
steps.note: A single version-controlled source replaces old copies, so nobody follows withdrawn rules.

steps.label: Review periodically and on triggers
steps.note: Planned reviews, plus triggers such as a new law, a major incident or a reorganization.

sequences.caption: Authority comes from the top; workability comes from consultation. A policy needs both before it is published.

sequences.title: The risk management cycle

steps.label: Board sets risk appetite
steps.note: A board-approved risk policy sets how much risk is acceptable and who is accountable.

steps.label: Identify risks from critical processes
steps.note: Start from key business processes and assets, then the threats and weaknesses facing each.

steps.label: Rate likelihood and impact
steps.note: Rate each risk before and after existing controls, using defined scales.

steps.label: Owner chooses a response
steps.note: Accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid, so the residual risk fits within appetite.

steps.label: Monitor and reassess continuously
steps.note: Track responses to completion; register serious new risks when they appear, not at the annual review.

sequences.caption: A register of rated risks is not a program. Value comes when owners treat risks and the results shape business decisions.

sequences.title: Retaining and disposing of records

steps.label: Set a period per category
steps.note: Each data category gets a retention period with a documented legal or business basis.

steps.label: Check for legal holds
steps.note: When the period ends, confirm no litigation or investigation hold applies before anything is deleted.

steps.label: Destroy every copy
steps.note: Use a method matched to the classification, including backups, archives and vendor-held copies.

steps.label: Keep proof of destruction
steps.note: Evidence shows what was destroyed, when and how, for auditors and regulators.

sequences.caption: Keep data as long as the law or the business needs it, and no longer. A legal hold always pauses disposal.

sequences.title: Designing a performance metric

steps.label: Identify critical success factors
steps.note: Name what must go right for the business objective to be achieved.

steps.label: Choose KPIs that measure them
steps.note: Each key performance indicator (KPI) tracks a success factor, not just IT activity.

steps.label: Agree one enterprise definition
steps.note: One calculation for everyone, so results can be compared or added up across units.

steps.label: Measure a baseline
steps.note: Record current performance from systems of record before setting any improvement target.

steps.label: Set independently approved targets
steps.note: Someone outside the measured team approves targets, which are never lowered just to stay green.

sequences.caption: A green dashboard proves nothing if the metric misses the objective, or if its data and targets come from the team being measured.

sequences.title: From idea to authorized project

steps.label: Define the problem and needs
steps.note: State the business problem and high-level needs before looking at any product or vendor.

steps.label: Study feasibility
steps.note: Test technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule angles, with assumptions recorded.

steps.label: Write the business case
steps.note: Options including doing nothing, lifetime costs, measurable benefits with baselines, and an owner per benefit.

steps.label: Approve the investment
steps.note: Management makes the go or no-go decision on the evidence.

steps.label: Sign the project charter
steps.note: The sponsor formally authorizes the project and delegates authority to a named project manager.

sequences.caption: The business case justifies the spending; the charter authorizes the work. Neither should start from a vendor demonstration.

sequences.title: Waterfall development, phase by phase

steps.label: Approve the requirements
steps.note: Business owners approve what the system must do; this baseline anchors every later phase.

steps.label: Design the solution
steps.note: Architecture, data, interfaces and controls are designed against the approved requirements.

steps.label: Build the system
steps.note: Developers write and configure code under version control.

steps.label: Test against requirements
steps.note: Testing proves each requirement was met, with results traced back to it.

steps.label: Implement in production
steps.note: The system goes live after accountable owners sign off its readiness.

steps.label: Run the post-implementation review
steps.note: After stable operation, check that benefits were realized and controls work.

sequences.caption: Waterfall runs each phase once, with a signed gate before the next. Without approved requirements, there is nothing to design or test against.

sequences.title: Buying software from a vendor

steps.label: Document the requirements
steps.note: Written business needs come before any vendor contact.

steps.label: Issue a request for proposal
steps.note: Scoring criteria and their weights are fixed before any proposal arrives.

steps.label: Shortlist by scored criteria
steps.note: Responses are scored against the preset weights; weights never change once proposals are opened.

steps.label: Demo with your own scenarios
steps.note: Shortlisted vendors run your business scenarios, and their references are checked.

steps.label: Sign a protective contract
steps.note: Service levels, right to audit, data ownership, exit terms, and verified escrow for critical code.

sequences.caption: Requirements and weighted criteria come first, so the most impressive demonstration cannot rewrite the rules after the fact.

sequences.title: Handling a project scope change

steps.label: Log a change request
steps.note: Every addition, however small, is recorded against the approved scope baseline.

steps.label: Analyze the impact
steps.note: Estimate the effect on cost, schedule, risk and benefits.

steps.label: Steering committee decides
steps.note: Management approves or rejects it; the project team never absorbs it informally.

steps.label: Update the project baselines
steps.note: Approved changes update the scope, schedule and budget baselines.

sequences.caption: Small additions add up to scope creep. Impact analysis first, then a management decision, then a new baseline.

sequences.title: Proving a data conversion

steps.label: Owner approves mapping rules
steps.note: The data owner, not IT alone, approves how each old field becomes a new one.

steps.label: Load and count every record
steps.note: Count records extracted, loaded and rejected; rejects are fixed and reloaded or formally written off.

steps.label: Reconcile counts and totals
steps.note: Match record counts, control totals and hash totals between source and target.

steps.label: Explain every difference
steps.note: Each variance is investigated and resolved; spot checks cannot prove completeness.

steps.label: Owner signs off acceptance
steps.note: The data owner accepts the converted data before go-live.

sequences.caption: Full reconciliation, every variance explained and owner sign-off prove a conversion is complete. Samples test accuracy, never completeness.

sequences.title: Handling an IT service outage

steps.label: Log and timestamp it
steps.note: The service desk, the single point of contact, records every incident.

steps.label: Set the priority
steps.note: Priority combines business impact and urgency.

steps.label: Restore service, even by workaround
steps.note: Get users working again first; open a problem record if the cause is unknown.

steps.label: User confirms it works
steps.note: User confirms service is back; major incidents are flagged for review before closure.

steps.label: Review major incidents
steps.note: For major incidents, a blameless review records facts; root cause and permanent fixes go to problem management.

sequences.caption: For an ordinary outage, restore first; root cause belongs to problem management. Security incidents differ: contain and eradicate before restoring.

sequences.title: Problem management: removing the cause

steps.label: Spot the recurring incidents
steps.note: Trend analysis links repeat incidents with a likely shared cause, and a problem record opens.

steps.label: Rebuild the timeline from data
steps.note: Monitoring data, not opinions, shows what actually happened and when.

steps.label: Find the root cause
steps.note: Look past human error to the process or tool weakness that allowed it.

steps.label: Record a known error
steps.note: Document the cause and a workaround for the service desk while the fix is prepared.

steps.label: Fix through change management
steps.note: The permanent fix is approved, tested and released like any other change.

steps.label: Confirm incidents have stopped
steps.note: Close only after monitoring shows the incidents have stopped for an agreed period.

sequences.caption: Incident management gets service back; problem management makes sure it does not fail the same way again.

sequences.title: Patching by risk

steps.label: Match patches to the inventory
steps.note: Vendor notices and threat feeds are checked against the asset inventory to find affected systems.

steps.label: Prioritize exploited, exposed flaws
steps.note: Active exploitation on exposed systems ranks ahead of raw severity scores.

steps.label: Test with a rollback plan
steps.note: Urgency shortens testing but never removes it; check dependent interfaces too.

steps.label: Deploy through change control
steps.note: Approved deployment, on a schedule set by risk.

steps.label: Scan to verify installation
steps.note: A deployment report is not proof; scans confirm each patch is actually installed.

sequences.caption: Patch by real risk, not by score or vendor order. A patch that must wait needs compensating controls and time-bound owner acceptance.

sequences.title: Invoking the disaster recovery plan

steps.label: Ensure everyone is safe
steps.note: The emergency response team ensures safety, limits the damage and alerts management.

steps.label: Assess the damage
steps.note: The damage assessment team judges the extent and advises whether to invoke.

steps.label: Invoke on set criteria
steps.note: The named authority or a delegated alternate declares at once when measurable thresholds are met.

steps.label: Restore shared infrastructure
steps.note: Directory, network and other shared services return before the applications that depend on them.

steps.label: Restore applications by priority
steps.note: Applications return in business impact analysis (BIA) order, adjusted for dependencies.

steps.label: Relocate to the permanent site
steps.note: The relocation team moves operations back to a restored or new permanent site.

sequences.caption: Invoke fast, under authority named in advance, then recover by business priority. Waiting for consensus or a missing executive must never delay it.

sequences.title: Continuity tests, simplest to riskiest

steps.label: Checklist review
steps.note: Check plan contents and contact details against current reality; nothing moves.

steps.label: Structured walkthrough
steps.note: The team talks a scenario through, step by step, to test roles and decisions.

steps.label: Simulation
steps.note: A realistic scenario plays out with timed events, without moving live processing.

steps.label: Parallel test
steps.note: Recovery systems process real data at the alternate site while production keeps running.

steps.label: Full-interruption test
steps.note: Production is shut down and moved to the recovery site: the most realistic and riskiest test.

sequences.caption: Build up realism and risk one step at a time. A full interruption comes only after simpler tests succeed.

sequences.title: Sanitizing media before reuse or disposal

steps.label: Choose clear, purge or destroy
steps.note: The method follows the data's sensitivity and whether the media will leave your control.

steps.label: Sanitize the media
steps.note: Apply a method suited to the media type, with custody records if a vendor handles it.

steps.label: Verify it worked
steps.note: A designated person confirms the data cannot be recovered.

steps.label: Record and close the asset
steps.note: Log the item, method, date and operator on a certificate, then close the asset record.

sequences.caption: Deleting or formatting is not sanitizing. Match the method to the data and its destination, then prove it with evidence.

sequences.title: Undoing a bad update to a point in time

steps.label: Restore backup to a spare server
steps.note: Restore to a separate server, so the damaged live database is left untouched.

steps.label: Roll the log forward
steps.note: Reapply committed changes from the transaction log up to just before the error.

steps.label: Verify the recovered copy
steps.note: Check the recovered data is complete and correct before it touches production.

steps.label: Copy back the correct data
steps.note: Replace only the damaged records in production, with the business owner's approval.

sequences.caption: A backup plus the transaction log recovers to a chosen point. Backup and log-copy frequency must meet the recovery point objective.

sequences.title: Managing vulnerabilities

steps.label: Discover every asset
steps.note: Automated discovery keeps the asset list complete, because systems nobody scans stay invisible.

steps.label: Run credentialed scans
steps.note: Scans that sign in see installed software and settings, not just open network services.

steps.label: Rank by exploitability and value
steps.note: Known exploitation, exposure and asset value outrank the severity score alone.

steps.label: Assign an owner and deadline
steps.note: Each finding gets a named owner and a risk-based due date.

steps.label: Verify the fix by scan
steps.note: Only the next scan proves the weakness is gone; repeat findings mean remediation is broken.

sequences.caption: A scan is only as good as its coverage, and a finding matters only once it is fixed and verified.

sequences.title: Running a penetration test

steps.label: Authorize scope in writing
steps.note: Management signs off the scope and rules of engagement before any testing starts.

steps.label: Discover the targets
steps.note: Testers map the systems and services inside the agreed scope.

steps.label: Attempt exploitation
steps.note: Testers try to exploit weaknesses, stopping if they find signs of a real intruder.

steps.label: Report the findings
steps.note: Findings are ranked by exploitability and the value of the assets exposed.

steps.label: Remediate and verify
steps.note: Owners remediate by a deadline, and a prompt retest confirms each critical fix.

sequences.caption: No written authorization, no test. And a test reduces risk only when its findings are fixed and a retest proves it.

sequences.title: A cryptographic key's life

steps.label: Generate inside a secure module
steps.note: Keys are created in a hardware security module (HSM) or managed key service, never in code.

steps.label: Use for encryption
steps.note: Each key has a set lifetime, based on its type and use.

steps.label: Rotate to a new key
steps.note: A new key takes over for fresh encryption once the cryptoperiod ends.

steps.label: Retain for decryption only
steps.note: Keep it under control, for decryption only, while the data it protects is retained.

steps.label: Destroy it securely
steps.note: Destroy the key only when the data it protects is no longer needed.

sequences.caption: Secure storage does not remove the need to rotate, and destroying a key too early makes its data unrecoverable forever.

sequences.title: Just-in-time privileged access

steps.label: Request elevation with a reason
steps.note: The administrator asks for specific rights for a specific task, from a separate admin account.

steps.label: Independent approval
steps.note: A person other than the requester approves; self-approved just-in-time (JIT) access is just self-service.

steps.label: Check out the vaulted credential
steps.note: The vault releases the password, so the administrator never needs to know it permanently.

steps.label: Work in a recorded session
steps.note: Recordings are stored where administrators cannot alter them.

steps.label: Access expires, password rotates
steps.note: Elevation ends automatically at the time limit, and the vault changes the password.

sequences.caption: Every elevation is approved by someone else, time-limited and recorded. Removing standing privilege is the point.

sequences.title: Cleaning up orphan accounts

steps.label: Match accounts to HR records
steps.note: Reconcile active accounts against human resources (HR) records to find leavers still enabled.

steps.label: Disable the orphan accounts
steps.note: Disable, do not delete: it stops the exposure and keeps the account and its logs as evidence.

steps.label: Check them for misuse
steps.note: Review activity since each person left for signs the account was used.

steps.label: Fix the HR-to-IT feed
steps.note: Repair the root cause, ideally with an automated, HR-driven removal trigger.

sequences.caption: Contain first, investigate second, then fix the process. Redesigning the feed while the accounts stay live leaves the door open.

sequences.title: Enforcing a security baseline

steps.label: Adapt a hardening guide
steps.note: Start from a guide such as the Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks, tuned to your risk.

steps.label: Build from an approved image
steps.note: New systems start compliant because they come from an approved template.

steps.label: Scan for configuration drift
steps.note: Automated scans compare live systems with the baseline and flag changes.

steps.label: Fix drift or record exception
steps.note: A system that cannot comply needs owner risk acceptance, an expiry date and a compensating control.

sequences.caption: A baseline is a floor, not a goal. Every gap is either fixed or covered by a time-limited, owned exception.
